questions.question: Which of the following is/are exempted from disclosure of information under Section 8 of the Right to Information Act, 2005?
statements: Information, disclosure of which would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India.
Information which has been expressly forbidden to be published by any court of law.
Information received in confidence from foreign governments.
questions.subTopic: Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 Exemptions
questions.concept: Statutory exemptions to transparency under Section 8(1) of the RTI Act.
questions.explanation: All three categories are explicitly exempted from disclosure under Section 8(1) of the RTI Act, 2005: 1. Section 8(1)(a) exempts information whose disclosure would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State. 2. Section 8(1)(b) exempts information which has been expressly forbidden to be published by any court of law or tribunal or the disclosure of which may constitute contempt of court. 3. Section 8(1)(f) exempts information received in confidence from foreign Governments.

statementAnalysis.text: Information, disclosure of which would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India.
statementAnalysis.why: Section 8(1)(a) statutory exemption.

statementAnalysis.text: Information which has been expressly forbidden to be published by any court of law.
statementAnalysis.why: Section 8(1)(b) statutory exemption.

statementAnalysis.text: Information received in confidence from foreign governments.
statementAnalysis.why: Section 8(1)(f) statutory exemption.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Statement 3 is also an explicit statutory exemption.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Statement 1 is also an explicit statutory exemption.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Statement 2 is also an explicit statutory exemption.
optionAnalysis.d: Correct: All three statements represent verified Section 8 exemptions.

questions.trap: A common trap is believing RTI has zero national security exemptions, whereas Section 8 contains 10 comprehensive exemption clauses (a to j).
relatedFacts: Under Section 8(2), a public authority may allow access to information if public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests.
Second Schedule of RTI Act exempts intelligence and security organizations (IB, RAW, DRI, NTRO) except regarding allegations of corruption and human rights violations.
Information must normally be provided within 30 days of application (or 48 hours if it concerns the life or liberty of a person).

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: With reference to the Ordinance-making power of the President of India under Article 123, which of the following statements is/are correct?
statements: The President can promulgate an ordinance only when both Houses of Parliament are not in session.
An ordinance promulgated by the President has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
questions.subTopic: Article 123 & Ordinance Making Power
questions.concept: Conditions for promulgating executive ordinances and legislative equivalence with Parliamentary statutes.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: The President can promulgate an ordinance when EITHER of the two Houses of Parliament is not in session (because a law requires passage by both Houses; if even one House is not in session, legislation cannot be enacted). It is NOT required that 'both' Houses must be prorogued. Statement 2 is correct: Under Article 123(2), an ordinance has the same legal force and effect as an Act of Parliament, subject to the same constitutional limitations. Statement 3 is correct: Under Article 123(2)(b), an ordinance may be withdrawn at any time by the President (on the advice of the Council of Ministers).

statementAnalysis.text: The President can promulgate an ordinance only when both Houses of Parliament are not in session.
statementAnalysis.why: Can be promulgated if even ONE House is not in session.

statementAnalysis.text: An ordinance promulgated by the President has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
statementAnalysis.why: Article 123(2) confirms parity of legal force with parliamentary statutes.

statementAnalysis.text: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
statementAnalysis.why: Article 123(2)(b) grants power to revoke or withdraw ordinances at any time.

optionAnalysis.b: Correct: Statements 2 and 3 are constitutionally valid.

questions.trap: Examiner writes 'only when both Houses are not in session', whereas an ordinance can be issued when either one or both Houses are prorogued.
relatedFacts: An ordinance ceases to operate six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament unless approved earlier.
Maximum life of an ordinance without parliamentary approval is 6 months and 6 weeks (since max interval between sessions is 6 months).
In D.C. Wadhwa (1987) and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), the Supreme Court ruled that re-promulgation of ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Under the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA), which of the following is/are the power(s) of the Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas?
statements: Ownership of minor forest produce.
Power to prevent alienation of land in Scheduled Areas and to restore any unlawfully alienated land of a Scheduled Tribe.
Mandatory consultation before making the acquisition of land in Scheduled Areas for development projects.
questions.subTopic: PESA Act, 1996 & Tribal Self-Rule
questions.concept: Statutory empowerment of Gram Sabhas to preserve tribal customary law, forest produce, and land rights.
questions.explanation: All three statements are central statutory provisions of the PESA Act, 1996 (enacted on the recommendations of the Bhuria Committee): 1. Section 4(m)(ii) explicitly endows the Gram Sabha and the Panchayats with the ownership of minor forest produce (MFP). 2. Section 4(m)(iii) grants the power to prevent alienation of land in the Scheduled Areas and to take appropriate action to restore any unlawfully alienated land of a Scheduled Tribe. 3. Section 4(i) mandates that the Gram Sabha or the Panchayats at the appropriate level shall be consulted before making the acquisition of land in the Scheduled Areas for development projects.

statementAnalysis.text: Ownership of minor forest produce.
statementAnalysis.why: Section 4(m)(ii) endows Gram Sabhas with ownership of MFP.

statementAnalysis.text: Power to prevent alienation of land in Scheduled Areas and to restore any unlawfully alienated land of a Scheduled Tribe.
statementAnalysis.why: Section 4(m)(iii) provides direct legal power to cancel illegal tribal land transfers.

statementAnalysis.text: Mandatory consultation before making the acquisition of land in Scheduled Areas for development projects.
statementAnalysis.why: Section 4(i) makes prior consultation with Gram Sabha compulsory.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 are also statutory powers.
optionAnalysis.d: Correct: All three statements represent verified PESA 1996 mandates.

questions.trap: Candidates might assume land acquisition is an exclusive domain of the State Revenue Department, forgetting PESA made Gram Sabha consultation mandatory in Fifth Schedule areas.
relatedFacts: PESA extends Part IX of the Constitution to the Fifth Schedule areas across 10 states (Andhra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, HP, Jharkhand, MP, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan).
Prior recommendation of the Gram Sabha is mandatory for granting prospecting licenses or mining leases for minor minerals in Scheduled Areas.
Every Gram Sabha is competent to safeguard and preserve the traditions, customs, cultural identity, community resources, and customary mode of dispute resolution.

questions.subTopic: Model Code of Conduct (MCC) Enforcement Timing
questions.concept: Immediate legal effect of MCC upon formal press conference announcement by the ECI.
questions.explanation: The Model Code of Conduct (MCC)—a set of consensus guidelines agreed upon by political parties to ensure free, fair elections and prevent the ruling party from misusing official machinery—comes into operational force IMMEDIATELY upon the formal press conference announcement of the election schedule by the Election Commission of India (ECI), and remains in force until the completion of the electoral process (counting and result declaration). This was confirmed by the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Harbans Singh Jalal (2001).

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: The statutory gazette notification occurs days/weeks after the initial schedule announcement.
optionAnalysis.b: Correct: MCC comes into force immediately when the Election Commission announces the dates.

questions.trap: Candidates confuse the formal statutory notification of election (under Sec 14/15 of RPA 1951) with the initial press announcement by ECI when MCC kicks in.
relatedFacts: The Model Code of Conduct does NOT have statutory backing; it is an informal code of ethics, though enforced by ECI through its constitutional powers under Article 324.
MCC was first introduced in Kerala in the 1960 State Assembly elections.
Once MCC comes into force, ministers cannot announce financial grants, lay foundation stones, or make promises of public projects.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which of the following is/are the principal feature(s) of the Government of India Act, 1919?
statements: Introduction of Dyarchy in the executive government of the provinces.
Introduction of separate communal electorates for Muslims.
Devolution of legislative authority by the Centre to the provinces.
questions.subTopic: Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms)
questions.concept: Dyarchy in provinces vs separate communal electorates for Muslims introduced in 1909.
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) introduced Dyarchy in the provinces by dividing provincial subjects into 'Transferred' (administered by ministers responsible to the legislature) and 'Reserved' (administered by the Governor and his executive council). It also devolved administrative and legislative subjects between Central and Provincial lists. Statement 2 is incorrect: Separate communal electorates for Muslims were introduced earlier by the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms), NOT the 1919 Act (the 1919 Act extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans, but did not 'introduce' it for Muslims).

statementAnalysis.text: Introduction of Dyarchy in the executive government of the provinces.
statementAnalysis.why: Dyarchy divided provincial governance into Transferred and Reserved subjects.

statementAnalysis.text: Introduction of separate communal electorates for Muslims.
statementAnalysis.why: Introduced in the 1909 Morley-Minto reforms, not 1919.

statementAnalysis.text: Devolution of legislative authority by the Centre to the provinces.
statementAnalysis.why: Separated Central and Provincial legislative subjects, granting provincial autonomy.

questions.trap: Examiner tests the chronological distinction between 'introduction' of communal electorates for Muslims (1909) vs their 'extension' to other minorities (1919).
relatedFacts: The 1919 Act introduced bicameralism at the Centre (Council of State and Legislative Assembly) for the first time.
It created the office of the High Commissioner for India in London.
It provided for the establishment of a Public Service Commission, leading to the Central Public Service Commission in 1926.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: With reference to the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India under Article 143, consider the following statements:
statements: The President of India can refer any question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for opinion.
The opinion expressed by the Supreme Court is binding on the President.
The Supreme Court is bound to give its opinion on any matter referred to it under Article 143(1).
questions.subTopic: Article 143 Advisory Jurisdiction
questions.concept: Discretionary nature of presidential advice and non-binding character of Supreme Court advisory opinions.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: Under Article 143(1), if at any time it appears to the President that a question of law or fact has arisen, or is likely to arise, which is of such a nature and of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the opinion of the Supreme Court, he may refer the question to that Court for consideration. Statement 2 is incorrect: The opinion expressed by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is purely advisory and consultative; it is NOT binding on the President or the Government. Statement 3 is incorrect: Under Article 143(1), the Supreme Court 'may' report its opinion to the President; it is NOT bound to give an opinion and can respectfully decline (as it did in the Special Reference regarding the Ayodhya dispute in 1994).

statementAnalysis.text: The President of India can refer any question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for opinion.
statementAnalysis.why: Direct text of Article 143(1).

statementAnalysis.text: The opinion expressed by the Supreme Court is binding on the President.
statementAnalysis.why: Advisory opinion is not a judicial decree and is not legally binding on the executive.

statementAnalysis.text: The Supreme Court is bound to give its opinion on any matter referred to it under Article 143(1).
statementAnalysis.why: The Court may decline to answer references under 143(1) (e.g. Ismail Faruqui / Ayodhya reference).

optionAnalysis.a: Correct: Only Statement 1 is constitutionally accurate.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Statements 2 and 3 are both false.

questions.trap: Note the critical distinction: Under Article 143(1) (general public importance), the Court is NOT bound to answer. Under Article 143(2) (pre-constitutional treaties), the Court 'shall' report its opinion (mandatory).
relatedFacts: References under Article 143 must be heard by a Constitution Bench comprising at least 5 judges (Article 145(3)).
Important references include: Delhi Laws Act (1951), Berubari Union (1960), Special Courts Bill (1978), and Presidential Poll (1974).
Advisory opinions do not constitute 'law declared by the Supreme Court' under Article 141 in the strict sense, but carry immense persuasive authority.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In the context of the Indian Constitution, which landmark judgment ruled that all laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, are open to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure?
questions.subTopic: Ninth Schedule Immunity & I.R. Coelho Ruling
questions.concept: End of blanket Ninth Schedule immunity for laws violating Fundamental Rights and the Basic Structure.
questions.explanation: In the landmark 9-judge Constitution Bench verdict in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Supreme Court unanimously held that laws included in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution are NOT immune from judicial review. Any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule on or after April 24, 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) will be judicially tested against the Basic Structure doctrine as reflected in Articles 14, 19, and 21.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Minerva Mills (1980) struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 that excluded judicial review.
optionAnalysis.b: Correct (Answer): I.R. Coelho (2007) settled the Ninth Schedule post-1973 judicial review doctrine.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Indra Sawhney (1992) established the 50% reservation ceiling and creamy layer principle.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Maneka Gandhi (1978) expanded Article 21 to include procedure that is just, fair, and reasonable.

questions.trap: Students often guess Kesavananda Bharati or Minerva Mills, but the specific Ninth Schedule retrospective review test was formulated in I.R. Coelho.
relatedFacts: The Ninth Schedule was originally added by the 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 along with Article 31B to protect agrarian land reforms.
Over 280 state and central laws are currently listed in the Ninth Schedule.
The Coelho ruling affirmed that judicial review is an integral constituent of the basic structure of the Constitution.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In the Constitution of India, promotion of international peace and security is included in the:
questions.subTopic: Article 51 & International Peace
questions.concept: Constitutional foreign policy mandate under Article 51 in Part IV.
questions.explanation: Article 51 of the Constitution of India, located in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy), directs the State to: (a) promote international peace and security; (b) maintain just and honourable relations between nations; (c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations; and (d) encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration. It forms the foundational constitutional basis of India's foreign policy and non-alignment.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Preamble speaks of fraternity and unity, not international peace directly.
optionAnalysis.b: Correct: Article 51 under DPSPs explicitly directs promotion of international peace and security.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Fundamental Duties pertain to citizens' duties toward the nation.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Ninth Schedule protects land reform laws from judicial review.

questions.trap: Candidates confuse the peaceful phrasing in the Preamble with the concrete foreign policy mandate in Article 51.
relatedFacts: Article 51 is a Liberal-Intellectual Directive Principle.
Article 51 does not give treaties self-executing force in domestic law; Parliament must enact domestic enabling legislation under Article 253 to implement international treaties.
India's Panchsheel principles and participation in UN Peacekeeping draw legitimacy from Article 51.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the election of the President of India:
statements: The value of the vote of an MLA of a State is calculated based on the population of the State as per the latest census.
The value of the vote of an MP is equal to the total value of votes of all the MLAs of all States divided by the total number of elected members of both Houses of Parliament.
Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament are part of the Electoral College.
questions.subTopic: Presidential Electoral College & Vote Weightage Formula (Articles 54 & 55)
questions.concept: Proportional representation by means of single transferable vote and 1971 census freeze.
questions.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: The population of the State used to calculate the value of an MLA's vote is NOT determined by the 'latest census'. By the 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001, the population of the States for presidential elections is frozen at the 1971 Census until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 are published. Statement 2 is correct: Under Article 55, the value of the vote of an MP is obtained by dividing the total value of votes assigned to all elected MLAs of all the States by the total number of elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha). Statement 3 is incorrect: Nominated members of Parliament do NOT participate in the election of the President (Article 54 restricts the Electoral College to ELECTED members of Parliament and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies).

statementAnalysis.text: The value of the vote of an MLA of a State is calculated based on the population of the State as per the latest census.
statementAnalysis.why: Frozen at the 1971 Census by the 84th Amendment until post-2026.

statementAnalysis.text: The value of the vote of an MP is equal to the total value of votes of all the MLAs of all States divided by the total number of elected members of both Houses of Parliament.
statementAnalysis.why: Exact statutory mathematical formula under Article 55(2)(c).

statementAnalysis.text: Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament are part of the Electoral College.
statementAnalysis.why: Only elected MPs and elected MLAs participate (nominated members participate only in impeachment).

optionAnalysis.b: Correct: Only Statement 2 is factually and mathematically correct.

questions.trap: Candidates overlook the 1971 census freeze mandated by the 84th Amendment, assuming current census data is used.
relatedFacts: Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi, Puducherry, and Jammu & Kashmir (UTs with assemblies) are part of the Electoral College (added by 70th Amendment Act, 1992).
Members of State Legislative Councils (MLCs) do NOT vote in the Presidential election under any circumstances.
Nominated members of Parliament DO participate in the impeachment of the President under Article 61, while State MLAs do NOT.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which one of the following Schedules of the Constitution of India contains provisions regarding Anti-Defection?
questions.subTopic: Tenth Schedule & Anti-Defection Law
questions.concept: Disqualification on ground of defection introduced by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.
questions.explanation: The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution contains the anti-defection provisions, inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985. It sets out the grounds on which a Member of Parliament or a State Legislative Assembly may be disqualified for defection: (1) voluntarily giving up party membership, (2) voting or abstaining contrary to party whip, (3) independent member joining any political party, or (4) nominated member joining a party after six months.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Second Schedule deals with salaries, allowances, and emoluments of constitutional dignitaries.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Fifth Schedule deals with administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Eighth Schedule enumerates the 22 officially recognized languages of India.
optionAnalysis.d: Correct (Answer): Tenth Schedule specifically contains the Anti-Defection provisions.

questions.trap: None; classic direct question testing mastery of the 12 Schedules of the Constitution.
relatedFacts: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act (2003) deleted the exemption clause for splits (one-third split) and capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the Lok Sabha/Assembly strength.
The Presiding Officer of the House decides disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule.
In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court held that the Presiding Officer acts as a tribunal and their decision is subject to judicial review.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) was introduced in India by:
questions.subTopic: Origins & Evolution of Public Interest Litigation (PIL)
questions.concept: Relaxation of the traditional doctrine of locus standi through judicial innovation.
questions.explanation: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) was not created by any statute or constitutional amendment; it was born in the late 1970s and early 1980s out of pioneering 'Judicial Initiative' and activism led by Supreme Court judges Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer. By diluting the rigid Anglo-Saxon doctrine of 'locus standi' (which required only the aggrieved party to approach the court), the Supreme Court allowed any public-spirited citizen or NGO to file petitions (even post-cards or letters) on behalf of marginalized, oppressed, or poor citizens whose fundamental rights were violated.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Parliament did not pass a PIL Act.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: PIL is not written in the constitutional text.
optionAnalysis.c: Correct: Pioneered judicially by Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer.

questions.trap: Assuming that major legal institutions must stem from formal statutory acts of Parliament rather than common-law judicial jurisprudence.
relatedFacts: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1979) is recognized as the first PIL case in India, leading to the release of over 40,000 undertrial prisoners.
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case, 1981) formally articulated the constitutional philosophy and liberalized locus standi of PIL.
The Supreme Court has issued strict guidelines to prevent frivolous 'private interest' litigations masquerading as public interest suits.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was established in 1964 on the recommendation of which Committee?
questions.subTopic: Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)
questions.concept: Founding of apex vigilance institution on Santhanam Committee recommendations and subsequent statutory status.
questions.explanation: The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was set up by the Government of India in February 1964 on the recommendations of the Committee on Prevention of Corruption, chaired by K. Santhanam. Originally established through an executive resolution, it was later conferred statutory status by Parliament through the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, making it an independent apex integrity and anti-corruption oversight body free from executive control.

optionAnalysis.a: Correct: Set up in 1964 on the recommendations of the K. Santhanam Committee (1962-64).
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: ARC (chaired by Morarji Desai) recommended the Lokpal and Lokayukta.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: A.D. Gorwala Committee (1951) reported on Public Administration in India.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: J.B. Kripalani Committee (1954-55) reported on Railway corruption.

questions.trap: Candidates often mix up the Santhanam Committee (which created the CVC) with the First ARC (which recommended Lokpal/Lokayukta).
relatedFacts: The CVC consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and not more than two Vigilance Commissioners.
They are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee consisting of the Prime Minister (Chair), Union Minister of Home Affairs, and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
They hold office for a term of 4 years or until they attain 65 years of age (whichever is earlier), and are ineligible for further government employment.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Article 30 of the Indian Constitution deals with the:

options.a: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
options.b: Right of minorities to establish and manage educational institutions
options.c: Cultural and educational rights of the majority community
options.d: Abolition of untouchability and prohibition of its practice

questions.subTopic: Article 30 & Minority Educational Rights
questions.concept: Protection of religious and linguistic minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.
questions.explanation: Article 30(1) of the Constitution grants all minorities, whether based on religion or language, the fundamental right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 30(2) forbids the State, in granting aid to educational institutions, from discriminating against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Article 25 covers freedom of conscience and religious profession.
optionAnalysis.b: Correct (Answer): Article 30 explicitly safeguards minority educational institutions.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Article 30 exclusively protects linguistic and religious minorities, not majority communities.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Article 17 deals with the abolition of untouchability.

questions.trap: Candidates confuse Article 29 (protection of language, script, or culture of any section of citizens) with Article 30 (institutional rights specifically of religious/linguistic minorities).
relatedFacts: The term "minority" is not defined anywhere in the Constitution of India.
In T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002), the Supreme Court ruled that for Article 30, minority status must be determined State-wise, not nationally.

Under the 44th Amendment Act (1978), Article 30(1A) was added to ensure that mandatory acquisition of minority institution property requires compensation that does not restrict their constitutional right.

questions.question: Which Commission was appointed in 1983 to examine and review the working of the existing arrangements between the Union and States in India?
questions.subTopic: Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations
questions.concept: Institutional review of Indian federal dynamics, Article 356 misuse, and Governor appointments.
questions.explanation: In June 1983, the Central Government appointed a three-member Commission under the chairmanship of Justice R.S. Sarkaria (retired Supreme Court judge) to examine and review the working of the existing arrangements between the Union and the States. The Sarkaria Commission submitted its comprehensive 247-recommendation report in 1988, advocating a strong Centre with cooperative federalism, establishing the Inter-State Council (Art 263), and using Article 356 only as a weapon of last resort ('measure of last resort').

optionAnalysis.a: Correct: Sarkaria Commission was constituted in 1983 (reported 1988).
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Punchhi Commission was constituted later in 2007 (reported 2010).
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Rajamannar Committee was appointed by Tamil Nadu Government in 1969.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Kothari Commission (1964-66) was an education commission.

questions.trap: Confusing the earlier Sarkaria Commission (1983) with the second Centre-State commission (Punchhi Commission, 2007).
relatedFacts: The Inter-State Council was formally established in 1990 by presidential order based on Sarkaria Commission recommendations.
The Sarkaria Commission recommended that a Governor should be an eminent person from outside the state, detached from local politics.
It opposed the abolition of All India Services, arguing they are essential for administrative unity and federal integration.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978, removed which one of the following rights from the category of Fundamental Rights?
questions.subTopic: Right to Property & Article 300A
questions.concept: Transition of Right to Property from Fundamental Right to ordinary legal/constitutional right.
questions.explanation: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 (enacted by the Janata Party government under Morarji Desai) repealed the Right to Property as a Fundamental Right by omitting Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from Part III. It inserted a new Article 300A in Part XII under the heading 'Right to Property', declaring: 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.' Consequently, the right to property is now a legal and constitutional right, but no longer a Fundamental Right.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Freedom of speech remains protected under Article 19(1)(a).
optionAnalysis.b: Correct (Answer): Right to Property was deleted from Part III by the 44th Amendment.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: Article 32 remains the cornerstone of Fundamental Rights.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) remains fundamental.

questions.trap: Aspirants assume property is now an unwritten right, forgetting it is still an explicit constitutional right under Article 300A.
relatedFacts: In case of violation of Article 300A, the aggrieved person cannot approach the Supreme Court directly under Article 32, but can move the High Court under Article 226.
The Supreme Court in several verdicts has held that property rights are also human rights.
The 44th Amendment also replaced the term 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' in Article 352.

questions.subTopic: Statutory Bodies (National Human Rights Commission)
questions.concept: Distinction between bodies established under constitutional Articles vs statutory parliamentary acts.
questions.explanation: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is NOT a constitutional body; it is a STATUTORY body established in October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. In contrast: 1. Election Commission of India is a constitutional body established under Article 324. 2. Finance Commission is a constitutional body constituted under Article 280. 4. Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) is a constitutional body established under Article 315.

statementAnalysis.text: Election Commission of India
statementAnalysis.why: Constitutional body under Article 324.

statementAnalysis.text: Finance Commission
statementAnalysis.why: Constitutional body under Article 280.

statementAnalysis.text: National Human Rights Commission
statementAnalysis.why: Statutory body established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

statementAnalysis.text: Union Public Service Commission
statementAnalysis.why: Constitutional body under Article 315.

optionAnalysis.b: Correct: Only NHRC is a statutory body not mentioned in the Constitution.

questions.trap: Aspirants assume high-profile commissions like NHRC, CVC, or CIC are in the Constitution.
relatedFacts: The Chairperson of the NHRC is a retired Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court.

The recommendation committee for appointing NHRC members is headed by the Prime Minister and includes the Speaker of Lok Sabha, Union Home Minister, Leaders of Opposition in both Houses, and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
NHRC has the powers of a civil court, but its recommendations are purely advisory and not binding on governments.

questions.question: Under Article 100(3) of the Constitution, the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament is:

options.a: One-tenth of the total number of members of the House
options.b: One-sixth of the total number of members of the House
options.c: One-eighth of the total number of members of the House
options.d: One-fifth of the total number of members of the House

questions.subTopic: Article 100 & Quorum Requirements
questions.concept: Minimum attendance threshold required to conduct parliamentary transactions (10% of total membership).
questions.explanation: Article 100(3) of the Constitution of India provides that until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth (10%) of the total number of members of the House. For Lok Sabha, this translates to 55 members (10% of 543), and for Rajya Sabha, it translates to 25 members (10% of 245). If at any time there is no quorum, it is the duty of the Chairman/Speaker to either adjourn the House or suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.

optionAnalysis.a: Correct: One-tenth (10%) is the constitutional quorum for both Houses of Parliament.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: One-sixth was an archaic colonial threshold.

questions.trap: Straightforward constitutional text; remember that the same 1/10th quorum rule applies to State Legislative Assemblies and Councils under Article 189(3).
relatedFacts: The 42nd Amendment Act (1976) omitted the quorum provisions, but the 44th Amendment Act (1978) restored them.
The quorum includes the presiding officer.
If the bell rings and no quorum is assembled, the presiding officer waits and then adjourns the House.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which one of the following statements regarding the Preamble to the Constitution of India is NOT correct?

options.a: It is not enforceable in a court of law.
options.b: The Supreme Court has held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution.
options.c: The Preamble can be amended under Article 368 of the Constitution.
options.d: The Preamble overrides the express provisions of the Constitution.

questions.subTopic: Legal Status & Enforceability of the Preamble
questions.concept: Non-justiciability and subordination of Preamble to express constitutional provisions.
questions.explanation: Statement (d) is NOT correct: The Preamble is an interpretive key to the minds of the Constitution-makers, but it does NOT confer any substantive legislative powers on legislatures, nor can it override or invalidate any express, substantive operative provisions of the Constitution. If there is a direct conflict between the Preamble and an unambiguous Article of the Constitution, the express Article prevails. Statements (a), (b), and (c) are correct: The Preamble is non-justiciable (a); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held it is an integral part of the Constitution (b); and it can be amended under Article 368 subject to the Basic Structure doctrine (c).

optionAnalysis.a: Correct statement: Preamble is non-justiciable and non-enforceable per se.
optionAnalysis.b: Correct statement: Overruled Berubari (1960) in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
optionAnalysis.c: Correct statement: Amended once by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976).
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect statement (Answer): Preamble cannot override express constitutional articles.

questions.trap: Thinking that because the Preamble is 'part of the Constitution', it carries substantive overriding force over other articles.
relatedFacts: In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Supreme Court originally opined that the Preamble is NOT a part of the Constitution.
The 42nd Amendment Act (1976) added three new words: 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity'.
The Preamble is based on the 'Objectives Resolution' drafted and moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on December 13, 1946.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: The concept of 'Welfare State' in the Indian Constitution is centered in:
questions.subTopic: Part IV & Socio-Economic Democracy
questions.concept: Directive Principles of State Policy as the constitutional charter of the Indian Welfare State.
questions.explanation: The concept of a 'Welfare State'—aiming to secure socio-economic justice, minimize inequalities in income and status, provide social security, and ensure the right to adequate means of livelihood—finds its primary institutional embodiment in the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36 to 51). Article 38 explicitly directs the State to 'promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life.'

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Preamble outlines the philosophical vision, but Part IV provides the operative welfare charter.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Fundamental Rights establish political democracy and negative state restraints.
optionAnalysis.c: Correct (Answer): DPSPs constitute the positive obligations of the state to build a welfare state.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Seventh Schedule deals with legislative competence.

questions.trap: Candidates confuse Political Democracy (guaranteed by Fundamental Rights) with Socio-Economic Democracy / Welfare State (enshrined in DPSPs).
relatedFacts: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar termed DPSPs as the 'novel features' of the Indian Constitution.
Granville Austin described Fundamental Rights and DPSPs together as the 'Conscience of the Constitution'.
DPSPs were borrowed from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had copied them from the Spanish Constitution.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides for the proclamation of Financial Emergency?
questions.subTopic: Article 360 & Financial Emergency
questions.concept: Proclamation, parliamentary approval, and fiscal consequences of Financial Emergency in India.
questions.explanation: Article 360 of the Constitution of India empowers the President to proclaim a Financial Emergency if he is satisfied that a situation has arisen whereby the financial stability or credit of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened. A proclamation of financial emergency must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within two months by a simple majority. During its operation, the executive authority of the Union can direct states to observe financial propriety, reserve money bills for President's consideration, and reduce the salaries of all public servants, including Supreme Court and High Court judges.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Article 352 deals with National Emergency (War, External Aggression, Armed Rebellion).
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Article 356 deals with President's Rule (Failure of constitutional machinery in states).
optionAnalysis.c: Correct (Answer): Article 360 specifically governs Financial Emergency.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Article 365 deals with failure of a state to comply with central directions.

questions.trap: Easy recall question, but note that Financial Emergency has NEVER been proclaimed in India to date (not even during the severe 1991 balance-of-payments crisis).

questions.question: The power of the Supreme Court of India to decide disputes between the Centre and the States falls under its:
questions.subTopic: Article 131 & Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
questions.concept: Exclusive competence of the Apex Court to adjudicate federal inter-governmental legal disputes.
questions.explanation: Under Article 131 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has exclusive 'Original Jurisdiction' to decide any dispute: (a) between the Government of India and one or more States; (b) between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other; or (c) between two or more States, if and in so far as the dispute involves any question (whether of law or of fact) on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Advisory jurisdiction falls under Article 143 (President seeking opinion).
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Appellate jurisdiction covers appeals from High Courts (Arts 132-134).
optionAnalysis.c: Correct (Answer): Exclusive Original Jurisdiction under Article 131.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Not a technical jurisdiction category in the Constitution.

questions.trap: Note that inter-state river water disputes do NOT fall under Article 131 original jurisdiction; they are barred by Article 262 and adjudicated by statutory River Water Tribunals.
relatedFacts: Original jurisdiction under Article 131 does not extend to pre-constitution treaties or agreements.
The dispute under Article 131 must involve a legal right, not a purely political disagreement.
Private citizens cannot invoke Article 131 against a State or the Centre.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: In the Interim Government formed in 1946, who among the following was the Vice-President of the Executive Council?
questions.subTopic: Interim Government Portfolio Allocation (1946)
questions.concept: De facto Prime Ministerial role of Jawaharlal Nehru in the Viceroy's Executive Council.
questions.explanation: The Interim Government of India was sworn in on September 2, 1946, pursuant to the Cabinet Mission Plan. The Viceroy of India (Lord Wavell, followed by Lord Mountbatten) served as the ex-officio President of the Executive Council, while Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru was designated as the Vice-President of the Council, essentially functioning as the de facto head of the government (Prime Minister) along with holding the portfolios of External Affairs and Commonwealth Relations.

optionAnalysis.a: Correct: Jawaharlal Nehru was Vice-President of the Executive Council and in charge of External Affairs.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Dr. Radhakrishnan was in academia and later became India's first Vice-President.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: C. Rajagopalachari held the Industries and Supplies portfolio.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was in charge of Food and Agriculture.

questions.trap: Candidates assume the head of the interim council had the formal title of 'Prime Minister' from day one; the constitutional title until August 1947 was 'Vice-President of the Executive Council'.
relatedFacts: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel held the portfolios of Home, Information and Broadcasting.
Liaquat Ali Khan of the Muslim League joined in October 1946 and held the crucial Finance portfolio.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was not part of the 1946 Interim Government, but became Law Minister in the post-independence 1947 Cabinet.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which one of the following Committees recommended conferring constitutional status on Panchayati Raj institutions in India?
questions.subTopic: Evolution of Panchayati Raj & L.M. Singhvi Committee
questions.concept: First formal recommendation for constitutional entrenchment of PRIs in 1986.
questions.explanation: In 1986, the Rajiv Gandhi government appointed a committee on 'Revitalisation of Panchayati Raj Institutions for Democracy and Development' under the chairmanship of Dr. L.M. Singhvi. The L.M. Singhvi Committee was the FIRST committee to unequivocally recommend that Panchayati Raj institutions should be constitutionally recognized, protected, and preserved by adding a new chapter to the Constitution. This recommendation paved the way for the 64th Amendment Bill (1989) and ultimately the landmark 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) recommended the 3-tier system ('Democratic Decentralisation'), but not constitutional status.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: Ashok Mehta (1977-78) recommended a 2-tier system (Mandal Panchayat + Zilla Parishad).
optionAnalysis.c: Correct (Answer): L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) first recommended constitutional entrenchment.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) focused on administrative arrangements for rural development ('grass without roots').

questions.trap: Aspirants frequently confuse Balwant Rai Mehta (the pioneer of PRIs) with L.M. Singhvi (who championed constitutional entrenchment).
relatedFacts: Rajasthan was the first state to establish Panchayati Raj (inaugurated at Nagaur on October 2, 1959 by Jawaharlal Nehru).
Thungon Committee (1988) also strongly supported L.M. Singhvi's recommendation for constitutional recognition.
The 73rd Amendment inserted Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (containing 29 functional items) into the Constitution.

questions.subTopic: Article 51A Enumeration & Non-Duties
questions.concept: Difference between civic/statutory actions and textually enumerated Fundamental Duties under Part IVA.
questions.explanation: Voting in public elections is a statutory/legal duty or civic responsibility, but it is NOT an enumerated Fundamental Duty under Article 51A. The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) had originally recommended that duty to pay taxes and casting vote should be made fundamental duties, but Parliament did NOT include them in the 42nd Amendment Act. Options (a) matches 51A(a), (b) matches 51A(g), and (d) matches 51A(h).

optionAnalysis.c: Correct (Answer): Casting vote in public elections is NOT a fundamental duty in Article 51A.

questions.trap: Candidates assume patriotic and good citizenship practices like voting or paying taxes are fundamental duties, whereas they are absent from Article 51A.
relatedFacts: Fundamental Duties were added to Part IVA of the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 on Swaran Singh Committee recommendations.
Originally 10 duties were inserted; the 11th duty (education for children 6-14) was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
Fundamental Duties were inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: Which one of the following was the biggest source for the Constitution of India?
questions.subTopic: Sources of the Indian Constitution & GOI Act 1935
questions.concept: Structural blueprint borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935.
questions.explanation: The Government of India Act, 1935 served as the primary administrative and structural blueprint for the Constitution of India. More than 250 provisions (nearly two-thirds of the Constitution) were adapted directly or with minor modifications from the 1935 Act, including the Federal Scheme, Office of the Governor, Judiciary, Public Service Commissions, Emergency Provisions, and Administrative Details.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: GOI Act 1919 introduced Dyarchy in provinces, but was not the primary structural source.
optionAnalysis.b: Correct: GOI Act 1935 provided the overarching structural framework, federal scheme, and administrative detail.
optionAnalysis.c: Incorrect: 1947 Act partitioned British India and transferred sovereign power, but contained little structural governance design.
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: US Constitution contributed Fundamental Rights, Judicial Review, and Preamble inspiration, not the bulk administrative framework.

questions.trap: Candidates often choose US or British Constitution because of fundamental rights or parliamentary democracy, forgetting the immense administrative bulk came directly from the 1935 Act.
relatedFacts: The 1935 Act proposed an All-India Federation consisting of Provinces and Princely States (which never materialized).
It abolished Dyarchy in the provinces and introduced Provincial Autonomy.
It established the Federal Court of India in 1937, the forerunner to the Supreme Court of India.

questions.subject: Polity
questions.question: A Joint Sitting of the Parliament is presided over by:

options.b: The Vice-President of India (Chairman of Rajya Sabha)

questions.subTopic: Article 108 & Article 118(4) Joint Sitting Protocol
questions.concept: Presidency of Joint Sitting of Parliament and exclusion of the Rajya Sabha Chairman.
questions.explanation: Under Article 118(4) of the Constitution of India, at a Joint Sitting of the two Houses of Parliament (summoned by the President under Article 108 to resolve legislative deadlock), the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides. If the Speaker is absent, the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides; if the Deputy Speaker is also absent, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides. The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Vice-President of India) NEVER presides over a joint sitting under any circumstances because he/she is not a member of either House of Parliament.

optionAnalysis.a: Incorrect: The President summons the joint sitting, but does not preside over it.
optionAnalysis.b: Incorrect: The Chairman of Rajya Sabha (Vice-President) can NEVER preside.
optionAnalysis.c: Correct (Answer): The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides under Article 118(4).
optionAnalysis.d: Incorrect: Prime Minister is the leader of the House, not the presiding officer.

questions.trap: Many candidates guess the Vice-President / Chairman of Rajya Sabha, unaware that they are explicitly barred from presiding over joint sittings.
relatedFacts: There have been only three occasions in independent India when a Joint Sitting was convened to pass a Bill: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill (1978), and Prevention of Terrorism Bill (POTA, 2002).
Joint sittings cannot be summoned for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills.
Decisions in a joint sitting are taken by a simple majority of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting.
